tldr: We propose a hierarchical RL control framework that combines directional end-effector compliance—continuously tunable from 100 to 600 N/m along each orthogonal axis—with selectable root external force-following and force-rejection modes. Even without wrist force sensors, the system achieves stable and compliant contact motions by synthesizing residual policies via MoE on top of a stiff whole-body tracking policy.
hero_caption: Overall system architecture of CEER2. In Stage 1, a stiff whole-body tracking policy is trained and frozen. In Stage 2, high-level residual policies are learned according to the commanded end-effector stiffness and root modes. During real-world deployment, pre-trained EE experts are analytically interpolated (MoE synthesis) in compliance space to achieve the commanded stiffness, applied concurrently with the root mode.
overview:
While whole-body motion control for humanoid robots has made remarkable progress recently, tasks involving physical interaction with humans or the environment still face a major bottleneck. Merely tracking target trajectories stiffly generates excessive contact forces, leading to falls or damage. Conversely, making the end-effectors universally soft in all directions sacrifices the motion accuracy required for the task. For instance, when writing on a whiteboard, the robot must yield softly along the surface-normal direction to absorb force, while staying stiff in-plane to accurately guide the pen tip. Furthermore, in loco-manipulation tasks, whether the robot's body (root) should resist an external disturbance or move along with a person's pull varies depending on the context.

To address this, the authors developed "CEER2," a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework integrating directional and continuously tunable end-effector (EE) compliance (stiffness $100$ to $600\,\mathrm{N/m}$) with root external force rejection and force following modes. Training a single neural network on various stiffness levels and external forces causes multi-task interference, preventing the robot from producing the intended stiffness. The authors resolved this with a two-stage design: first establishing a robust, stiffly tracking low-level policy, and then layering high-level residual policies on top to introduce compliance. For the end-effectors, ten anchor experts are analytically blended via Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) through linear interpolation in compliance space (the inverse of stiffness), achieving arbitrary orthotropic stiffness without any additional training.

Along with rigorous perturbation tests in simulation, real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid (without 6-axis wrist force sensors) demonstrated online stiffness tuning, the benefits of directional compliance, and concurrent coordination with root damping across whiteboard writing, drawing straight lines under disturbances, yoga ball grasping, and collaborative carrying with a human.
contributions: Formulated a structured framework combining orthogonal, continuously tunable EE stiffness (100–600 N/m) for manipulation with selectable root compliance (one force rejection mode and two force-following damping modes) for locomotion.

Developed a gate-free MoE architecture that layers high-level residual policies over a frozen, stiff low-level whole-body tracking policy and analytically interpolates EE experts linearly in compliance space.
Estimated external forces from proprioceptive history without wrist force sensors, demonstrating directional stiffness control and human-robot collaborative carrying on a physical humanoid.

sections.heading: Why do humanoids need directional compliance?
sections.summary: While whole-body trajectory tracking has advanced, tasks with physical contact require flexibility to yield to external forces. This section outlines the motivation and challenges behind decoupling and unifying directional EE stiffness adjustment and root behavioral modes into a new compliance framework.
sections.details:
Humanoid whole-body control has seen enormous progress, enabling highly accurate tracking of complex motions. However, in tasks involving contact with the environment or humans, stubbornly tracking trajectories with high stiffness generates excessive contact forces, which can cause the robot to fall over or damage objects.

Conventional compliance control methods have predominantly focused on making the end-effector isotropically soft. While this reduces contact forces, it also degrades trajectory tracking accuracy along the axes where precision is actually needed. Consider writing on a board: the normal direction to the board must be soft (low stiffness) to relieve contact force, but the in-plane axes along the board must remain stiff (high stiffness) to trace characters accurately. Furthermore, the required stiffness values vary by task, and the robot's torso (root) may need to switch between resisting an external push and compliant following when pulled by a human.

Attempting to learn all of these behaviors in a single policy leads to severe multi-task interference across stiffness values and force directions, causing the policy to fail at reproducing commanded stiffnesses. To overcome this, the authors organize the functional roles into manipulation (EE) and locomotion (root), proposing a two-stage hierarchical reinforcement learning pipeline that adds residual commands over a stiff low-level tracking policy.

sections.heading: How does this differ from prior work? Directional stiffness and root behavior in focus
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work in humanoid compliance control, force/tactile sensing, and contact-aware motion generation. CEER2 is positioned as the only method that simultaneously addresses directional orthogonal stiffness tuning and root locomotion behaviors.
sections.details:
To clarify its positioning, the paper surveys related work from three perspectives:

### II-A Humanoid Compliance Control
Recent years have seen various compliant control approaches, such as GentleHumanoid, CHIP, SoftMimic, and CEER. However, most make the end-effector uniformly soft in all directions or are tailored to specific tasks. This work is the first to formulate directional compliance with independent stiffness across orthogonal axes, combined with a broad continuous tuning range and root locomotion responses.

### II-B Force and Tactile-Aware Interaction
To improve robustness against disturbances, incorporating external force and tactile feedback has gained traction. While estimating external forces from proprioception (joint positions, velocities, etc.) has matured, simply estimating contact forces does not automatically define what compliant behavior should be produced or how the robot should respond.

### II-C Contact-Aware Loco-Manipulation
Other approaches explicitly plan or imitate contact schedules and locations (e.g., OmniContact, ContactMimic). The proposed method does not compete with these motion generators; rather, it specifies the compliant response characteristics—how the robot relieves or follows forces across axes and at the root the instant contact occurs—making it complementary to existing planners.

sections.heading: Two-stage hierarchical learning and stiffness synthesis via analytical MoE
sections.summary: This section explains the architecture: freezing a stiff low-level whole-body tracking policy and placing high-level residual policies on top. End-effector stiffness is synthesized by analytically interpolating 10 experts in compliance space, while root modes are selected across three states, achieving interference-free compliant control.
sections.details:
The core of this method lies in its hierarchical formulation and analytical Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) designed to prevent multi-task interference.

### III-A & III-B EE Stiffness and Root Mode Definitions
The target EE displacement is defined from the nominal position $\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{nom},b}$, external force $\mathbf{f}^b$, and commanded orthogonal stiffness matrix $\mathbf{K}=\operatorname{diag}(K_x, K_y, K_z)$ as $\Delta\mathbf{x}^{*,b} = (f_x/K_x, f_y/K_y, f_z/K_z)$. The stiffness range is $100$ to $600\,\mathrm{N/m}$.
For the root, three modes are defined: a "Resistance" mode that braces against external forces, and two "Damping" modes ($B=60\,\mathrm{N\,s/m}$ low damping and $B=200\,\mathrm{N\,s/m}$ high damping) that yield and move continuously under force. Defining following in velocity rather than position (via damping) allows the robot to walk smoothly and continuously while being pulled.

### III-C Stage 1: Training the Stiff Low-Level Whole-Body Tracking Policy
First, the foundational low-level policy is trained. Using the AMASS dataset, a policy that stiffly tracks EE and root keypoint commands is constructed using PPO and Teacher-Student training. By injecting perturbing forces into upper-body links during training and teaching the policy to hold target trajectories firmly without losing balance, it becomes a dependable, stiff backbone upon which high-level compliance can be layered.

### III-D Stage 2: Training High-Level Residual Policies
The low-level policy is completely frozen. The high-level policies output residual offsets added to the low-level position commands. Instead of forcing a single network to learn every stiffness level, ten specialized experts are trained separately: one isotropic expert at $600\,\mathrm{N/m}$, and nine directional experts covering $100, 200, 400\,\mathrm{N/m}$ along each orthogonal axis. For real-world deployment without wrist sensors, a supervised estimator head is trained simultaneously to predict external forces from proprioceptive history.

### III-E Deployment: Analytical Compliance-Space MoE
This is a particularly elegant design. When running on hardware, rather than using a learned gating network, the outputs of the experts are blended analytically through linear interpolation in compliance space $C_d = 1/K_d$. Since displacement scales as $\Delta x = f \times C$, weighting in compliance space (inverse stiffness) allows neighboring anchor experts to produce accurate intermediate stiffnesses. Root modes are selected discretely, and because EE and root residuals target distinct command channels, they can be executed concurrently without conflict-resolution priority rules.

captions.F2: Training and deployment pipeline of the proposed method. In Stage 1, a fixed stiff tracking policy is established; in Stage 2, residual policies are trained. During deployment, ten pre-trained EE experts are blended using compliance-space weights and combined with the selected root mode before passing commands to the low-level policy.

sections.heading: Simulation evaluations and physical humanoid demonstrations
sections.summary: Rigorous stiffness error evaluations in simulation demonstrated the superiority of the hierarchical architecture and analytical MoE. Furthermore, using a physical Unitree G1, the framework validated directional stiffness during writing and achieved loco-manipulation in collaborative box carrying with a human.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted both in Isaac Sim simulation and on a physical humanoid (Unitree G1, no force sensors, inference running on an RTX 4080 laptop).

### IV-B Low-Level Policy Selection
Comparing tracking policies trained with different maximum perturbation forces, the 3-kp policy trained with 30 N disturbances exhibited an apparent stiffness of approximately $600\,\mathrm{N/m}$ and achieved the lowest nominal trajectory error. Increasing perturbation force to 60 N degraded tracking error, so the 30 N version was adopted as the frozen backbone.

### IV-C End-Effector Compliance Evaluation
A total of 960 pulling trials across 16 stiffness configurations (combining soft, stiff, and intermediate axes) were conducted.
- The proposed Analytical MoE achieved a compliance matrix error of $0.278$, a stiffness MAPE of $0.249$, and the slope relating commanded to measured stiffness (ideal = 1.0) was closest to 1.0, accurately controlling stiffness over the wide range.
- In contrast, the baseline that fed stiffness into a single high-level policy (Stiffness-conditioned HL) had a slope of only $0.136$, suffering from range compression (multi-task interference) where all outputs collapsed toward a middle value regardless of the command.
- Remarkably, the proposed MoE with estimated forces outperformed an ideal baseline (Oracle-force LL) that computed analytical offsets using ground-truth forces ($0.0349\,\mathrm{m}$ vs $0.0459\,\mathrm{m}$ tracking error). This occurs because the high-level policy learns to compensate not just for external forces, but also for closed-loop dynamic imperfections in the low-level controller.

### IV-D Root Compliance Evaluation
Evaluating external forces applied to the pelvis from front, back, and sides, the Resistance mode suppressed displacement best, while Low Damping ($B=60$) and High Damping ($B=200$) achieved their target velocity adjustments faithfully. Adding foot placement and yaw residual commands further reinforced root resistance.

### IV-E Real-World Demonstrations
Hardware experiments on the G1 demonstrated clear capabilities:
- **Online Stiffness Tuning**: When pulling the EE by 2 inches using a spring scale under commands of $K_y=100, 200, 600\,\mathrm{N/m}$, measured stiffness clearly modulated to $214.6, 338.6, 551\,\mathrm{N/m}$. Grasping compliance was also demonstrated by varying indentation depths into a yoga ball.
- **Directional Stiffness Writing**: In writing an "8" on a whiteboard, an isotropically soft setting caused the pen to lift and skip strokes, while an isotropically stiff setting broke the 3D-printed pen holder. Setting low stiffness only along the normal axis ($K_z=100\,\mathrm{N/m}$) while keeping in-plane axes stiff produced clean figures without breaking the tool.
- **Collaborative Carrying**: In co-carrying a 3 kg box with a human, the robot set soft lateral EE stiffness to absorb human movement discrepancies, high vertical stiffness to support the load, and root damping mode to follow the walking human, successfully completing collaborative walking without dropping the load.

The 3-kp stiff policy of this work (shown in blue) reaches a median stiffness around 600 N/m, serving as a solid foundation for high-level residual policies to synthesize compliance.

sections.heading: Conclusions and next steps: Toward smoother whole-body contact
sections.summary: The paper established a unified framework handling directional EE stiffness and root force following/rejection. The authors also clearly point out existing limitations, including low-level policy performance ceilings and stepping smoothness.
sections.details:
This work proposed a practical framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that combines orthogonal, continuously tunable EE stiffness with selectable root force following and rejection modes. By freezing a low-level whole-body tracking policy and blending high-level residual policies analytically in compliance space, the system prevents multi-task interference while enabling online switching on physical hardware.

At the same time, the authors candidly discuss several limitations:
- **Dependence on Low-Level Tracking**: Because high-level controllers only modify commands sent to the low-level policy, achievable capabilities are constrained by the underlying tracking performance. In particular, the low-level policy exhibits lower raw stiffness along the forward ($x$) direction, limiting the upper bound of achievable stiffness.
- **Stepping Smoothness**: While root damping successfully yields to external forces, walking can appear clunky and heavy, and active adaptation of foot placement relative to external loads remains incomplete.
Future directions include incorporating contact-aware foot placement targets and gait regularizations that penalize transition impacts, aiming for more natural and fluid whole-body compliance.

takeaways: When learning continuous stiffness with RL, training anchor experts and analytically interpolating in compliance space (inverse stiffness) prevents multi-task interference and achieves far higher accuracy than conditioning a single policy on stiffness inputs.

Adopting a two-stage architecture—first building a robust, stiff low-level tracking controller and then adding residual policies for compliance—effectively decouples locomotion stability from contact adaptability.

In physical humanoid contact tasks (such as writing or collaborative carrying), directional stiffness control—yielding along axes that absorb contact while remaining stiff along axes requiring precision or load support—is essential rather than being uniformly soft in all directions.
limitations: The upper bound of EE stiffness and dynamic response are heavily constrained by the capabilities of the underlying low-level whole-body policy (especially its raw stiffness limits along specific axes).
Locomotion in root damping mode remains somewhat clunky, lacking proactive foot placement adjustments based on external loads and smooth ground impact transitions.
EE stiffness control is limited to the range of 100 to 600 N/m, which does not cover tasks requiring extreme softness or exceptionally high stiffness.
